note: Prototype contribution data is active while the persistent backend is being wired.

contributions.title: Founder-submitted test record: CAQH Index gives the card an administrative burden anchor
contributions.body: Founder-submitted test evidence record: the CAQH Index is useful because it gives the healthcare card a concrete administrative-transaction lens instead of leaving simplification as a general efficiency claim. The source-link supports keeping eligibility, prior authorization, claims, and related workflow automation inside the evidence layer while still requiring the card to prove net savings and patient-facing benefit.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as founder-submitted source-linked evidence for the administrative simplification claim. The source strengthens the card's evidence layer while preserving pressure to distinguish transaction automation from verified total-cost savings.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Administrative transaction burden can be measured and targeted
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Use as an evidence anchor for administrative transaction burden, not as a conclusion that simplification alone captures savings for patients or clinicians.

providers.summary: The source is a strong structuring source because it gives the card a transaction-level administrative burden frame. It should attach to evidence and narrow the claim toward measurable workflow domains.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Administrative transaction burden can be measured and targeted
providers.reviewerNote: Treat as evidence that administrative simplification is measurable, not as proof of final net savings.

providers.summary: The source improves the card by anchoring administrative simplification in concrete transaction categories. Its weakness is that transaction burden does not automatically establish patient-facing savings, so that caveat should remain visible.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Administrative transaction burden can be measured and targeted
providers.reviewerNote: Good evidence anchor if paired with a caveat about net savings and distribution of benefits.

review.assignedToLabel: Administrative transaction burden can be measured and targeted
review.publicRecordNote: Incorporated as the first non-prototype, founder-submitted healthcare record. It strengthens the evidence layer by grounding administrative simplification in measurable transaction burden while preserving the open question of who captures savings.
review.decisionReason: Accepted as founder-submitted test evidence because the source gives the card a concrete administrative burden anchor readers can inspect through the evidence-attachment pathway.
review.reviewerNote: Keep this visible as founder-submitted evidence, not outside public usage. The card should still ask whether transaction savings become patient, clinician, or system-level benefit.

contributions.topicTitle: Public Review Stake for Institutional Claims
contributions.title: A sponsor could still control the review by narrowing the question
contributions.body: Prototype example: even if sponsors cannot buy the conclusion, they might still shape the review by defining the room too narrowly, excluding the hardest objections, or framing the success criteria around favorable evidence. The model needs an explicit scope challenge before money enters the review process.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as a core objection to the Public Review Stake model. The contribution pressures the difference between paying for scrutiny and quietly shaping the boundaries of scrutiny.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Sponsors may control scope even without controlling conclusions
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Keep visible near the revenue firewall and any institutional pilot explanation.

providers.summary: This is a clean objection because it identifies a capture path that survives the stated firewall. It should attach to scope-setting and review conditions.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Sponsors may control scope even without controlling conclusions
providers.reviewerNote: Use as a test for any pilot intake terms.

providers.summary: The objection is strong because it attacks process design rather than motives. A sponsor can distort a review without ever demanding a friendly final score.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Sponsors may control scope even without controlling conclusions
providers.reviewerNote: Require visible scope constraints and challenge rights.

review.assignedToLabel: Sponsors may control scope even without controlling conclusions
review.publicRecordNote: Accepted as a standing objection: the model must disclose and challenge sponsor scope constraints, not only final conclusions.
review.decisionReason: Kept visible because scope capture is one of the cleanest ways a review-stake model could fail.
review.reviewerNote: Attach to revenue firewall and pilot terms.

contributions.topicTitle: Public Review Stake for Institutional Claims
contributions.title: Funder identity and review constraints need to be visible before the room launches
contributions.body: Prototype example: the Public Review Stake model becomes more credible if sponsor identity, funding purpose, review constraints, and non-control terms are visible before a room begins. Disclosure after publication is weaker because readers cannot tell whether the process was already shaped upstream.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as a nuance that changes the model by moving disclosure earlier in the process. It turns funder transparency from an after-the-fact note into a launch condition.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Disclosure must precede sponsored room launch
aiIntake.reviewerNote: This should alter the card's operating condition for institutional pilots.

providers.summary: This contribution should attach to the assumption layer because it specifies a process precondition. The model is stronger if disclosure happens before review begins.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Disclosure must precede sponsored room launch
providers.reviewerNote: Good operational constraint for pilot inquiry flow.

providers.summary: This is not just a transparency preference; it affects whether readers can evaluate process independence. Late disclosure may be too late to preserve trust.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Disclosure must precede sponsored room launch
providers.reviewerNote: Make pre-launch disclosure part of the trust model.

review.assignedToLabel: Disclosure must precede sponsored room launch
review.publicRecordNote: Changed the card by making sponsor identity and review constraints a pre-launch condition, not merely a post-publication disclosure.
review.decisionReason: Incorporated because the timing of disclosure materially affects whether the Public Review Stake can resist capture.
review.reviewerNote: Carry this into /institutions and pilot inquiry language.

contributions.topicTitle: Public Review Stake for Institutional Claims
contributions.title: Reviewer selection and appeal rights remain unresolved
contributions.body: Prototype example: the model still needs a clearer reviewer-selection rule. If Civic Logos alone chooses reviewers, it may become the authority it is trying not to sell. If sponsors can choose reviewers, the firewall weakens. The open design question is how reviewers are selected, challenged, replaced, and audited.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as an implementation concern and open question. The contribution identifies reviewer selection as a governance dependency that must be designed before the model can scale.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: How should reviewers be selected, challenged, and audited?
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Strong enough to hold open, but not yet resolved into a concrete governance rule.

providers.summary: This should attach to the open-question layer because it names the governance bottleneck behind review legitimacy.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: How should reviewers be selected, challenged, and audited?
providers.reviewerNote: Needs a concrete reviewer governance model before incorporation.

providers.summary: The concern is important because reviewer selection is where the model either becomes trustworthy infrastructure or a new gatekeeping layer.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: How should reviewers be selected, challenged, and audited?
providers.reviewerNote: Hold as unresolved pressure on governance design.

review.assignedToLabel: How should reviewers be selected, challenged, and audited?
review.publicRecordNote: Held as an unresolved governance question: reviewer selection and appeal rights need a clearer rule before the model scales.
review.decisionReason: Marked needs review because the concern is central but not yet specific enough to revise the mechanism.
review.reviewerNote: Next pass should propose a reviewer-selection and challenge workflow.

contributions.title: Administrative cleanup may leave hospital and drug price power untouched
contributions.body: Administrative simplification may remove billing friction without materially changing hospital pricing leverage, specialist market concentration, or pharmaceutical pricing power. If those cost centers remain intact, the card should not imply that workflow reform alone can bend the total system cost curve very far.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as a durable objection to the card's savings thesis. The contribution argues that administrative reform may lower friction while leaving the largest pricing levers outside the proposal's reach.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Administrative simplification may not resolve hospital or pharmaceutical price leverage
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Keep visible against any claim that simplification alone solves overall cost inflation.

providers.summary: This is a clean objection-lane contribution because it forces the card to separate workflow waste from market power. It should attach to the main cost-savings claim rather than being treated as a side comment.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Administrative simplification may not resolve hospital or pharmaceutical price leverage
providers.reviewerNote: Good pressure against overclaiming total-cost impact.

providers.summary: The strongest feature of this contribution is that it targets the proposal's likely overreach rather than its weakest form. Savings may be real but still strategically insufficient if concentrated price power remains untouched.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Administrative simplification may not resolve hospital or pharmaceutical price leverage
providers.reviewerNote: Preserve as a live objection unless the topic card directly answers the price-power problem.

review.assignedToLabel: Administrative simplification may not resolve hospital or pharmaceutical price leverage
review.publicRecordNote: Kept visible as a standing objection: lowering paperwork alone may not materially reduce costs if hospital and pharmaceutical pricing power remains untouched.
review.decisionReason: Accepted into the objection lane so the card does not overclaim cost relief from administrative reform alone.
review.reviewerNote: Keep tied to the main thesis until the room has a stronger answer on hospitals, specialist networks, and pharmaceuticals.

contributions.title: Administrative overhead is materially significant and worth a direct pilot
contributions.body: A serious evidence contribution should keep the room anchored to the possibility that administrative overhead is large enough to justify focused testing. If a meaningful share of healthcare spending and clinician time is consumed by claims handling, prior authorization, and documentation churn, the card is right to treat simplification as a non-trivial reform lever.

evidenceSource.label: Health Affairs: Slowing the growth of health care spending

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as evidence supporting the claim that administrative overhead is large enough to justify direct testing. Both assisted readers treat it as a strengthening input rather than as a conclusive proof of savings.
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Use as baseline support while keeping the evidence burden high on measured savings.

providers.summary: This contribution strengthens the card's starting claim that paperwork burden is not trivial noise. It belongs in the evidence layer because it justifies testing the topic rather than proving the full proposal.
providers.reviewerNote: Good evidence anchor for why the topic is worth examining.

providers.summary: The contribution is useful because it narrows the claim: administrative burden may be large enough to matter, but the room still has to show where savings are real, durable, and clinically meaningful.
providers.reviewerNote: Keep as support for the room's evidence layer, not as license for overclaiming.

review.publicRecordNote: Added to the evidence layer as baseline support that administrative overhead is large enough to justify direct simplification pilots.
review.decisionReason: Incorporated into the evidence layer because it strengthens the case that administrative waste is large enough to test directly.
review.reviewerNote: Use this as a baseline reference, but continue separating insurer overhead from provider workflow waste.

contributions.title: Transition costs may consume the first years of projected savings
contributions.body: Even if the steady-state model is cleaner, early savings may be consumed by software migration, retraining, contract rewrites, temporary dual workflows, and local implementation failure. The card should pressure-test whether the proposal's timing assumptions are realistic rather than counting gross administrative savings as if the transition were free.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as an economic assumption challenge focused on timing rather than direction. The contribution argues that implementation friction could consume the first wave of nominal savings.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Transition costs stay below early administrative savings
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Strong enough to hold open, but still needs quantified transition modeling.

providers.summary: This belongs in the economic assumption challenge lane because it attacks the timing logic of the proposal. It should attach to the cost-savings assumptions and the economic-delta read.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Transition costs stay below early administrative savings

providers.summary: The contribution is important because many reform models confuse long-run plausibility with near-term fiscal credibility. Early implementation drag may determine whether the reform is survivable at all.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Transition costs stay below early administrative savings
providers.reviewerNote: Treat as a real stress test on the card's economic optimism.

review.assignedToLabel: Transition costs stay below early administrative savings
review.publicRecordNote: Holding open the question of whether transition costs could absorb early savings before the new model stabilizes.
review.decisionReason: Marked needs review because the challenge is strong, but the room still needs a comparable implementation model before changing the current read.
review.reviewerNote: Hold this against the economic-delta section until the card has a firmer transition-cost model.

contributions.title: AI triage helps only if human-escalation thresholds are explicit
contributions.body: AI-assisted triage may be genuinely useful for routine routing, intake normalization, and low-risk redirection. But the card should treat it as bounded support, not autonomous judgment. Hard human-escalation thresholds, override ownership, and auditability need to be part of the design or the triage layer becomes a new clinical risk instead of a workflow improvement.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as nuance with implementation implications. The contribution narrows the AI claim by requiring explicit escalation thresholds and human override design.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: AI triage is safe only if escalation thresholds and human override paths are explicit
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Useful because it improves the card without collapsing into generic anti-AI skepticism.

providers.summary: This contribution fits the nuance lane and should attach to the card's mechanism and assumptions. It improves the proposal by turning AI triage from a broad promise into a bounded workflow tool.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: AI triage is safe only if escalation thresholds and human override paths are explicit
providers.reviewerNote: Good narrowing move that makes the topic more governable.

providers.summary: The strength of this contribution is that it rescues the proposal from vague automation optimism. It identifies the boundary condition that determines whether AI triage is a support layer or a liability generator.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: AI triage is safe only if escalation thresholds and human override paths are explicit
providers.reviewerNote: Preserve as a first-order design constraint, not a footnote.

review.assignedToLabel: AI triage is safe only if escalation thresholds and human override paths are explicit
review.publicRecordNote: Changed the card by turning the AI triage layer into a bounded workflow that requires hard human-escalation thresholds.
review.decisionReason: Incorporated because it converts the AI layer from generic efficiency language into a bounded safety condition.
review.reviewerNote: Future revisions should specify escalation triggers, audit paths, and manual override ownership.

contributions.title: Paperwork reduction matters only if time actually returns to care teams
contributions.body: A provider-facing perspective should ask whether reduced clicks, fewer forms, or faster intake actually give time back to nurses, physicians, and coordinators. If reclaimed minutes are immediately reabsorbed into new compliance tasks or higher throughput demands, the card may mistake administrative rearrangement for real clinical relief.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as a personal/provider perspective with measurable operational implications. The contribution argues that savings claims should be tested against time actually returned to care teams.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: How should the room measure whether simplification returns time to clinical care rather than to new compliance demands?
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Good contribution, but it needs a sharper measurement frame before it can move the card.

providers.summary: This fits the personal-perspective lane while still giving the room a measurable operational question. It should attach to the open-question layer around how savings are defined and verified.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: How should the room measure whether simplification returns time to clinical care rather than to new compliance demands?
providers.reviewerNote: Invite follow-up on staffing metrics and workflow measurement.

providers.summary: The contribution is useful because it resists abstract efficiency claims and asks where recovered capacity actually lands. Without that check, the proposal could look humane while merely increasing throughput pressure.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: How should the room measure whether simplification returns time to clinical care rather than to new compliance demands?
providers.reviewerNote: Keep the perspective visible even before the room has a settled metric.

review.assignedToLabel: How should the room measure whether simplification returns time to clinical care rather than to new compliance demands?
review.publicRecordNote: Keeping open the provider-side question of whether paperwork reduction actually returns measurable time to clinical care teams.
review.decisionReason: Left pending because the perspective is strong, but the card still needs a clearer measurement standard before the contribution can alter the current read.
review.reviewerNote: Keep in the visible record and ask the next provider-facing contribution to translate this into measurable time-back criteria.
